inputs.original_text: They’re turning Harry Wait into the story so nobody has to confront what he was trying to expose: he requested ballots in the names of Robin Vos and Cory Mason to demonstrate that Wisconsin’s voter registration system could be exploited. The jury convicted him on two misdemeanor election fraud charges and one felony identity theft charge, while acquitting him of a second identity theft count. That split outcome lets officials claim the system is secure while punishing someone who tested it. The trial looks less like a warning about election vulnerabilities than a message about what happens when you make those vulnerabilities visible.
inputs.modified_text: They’ve made Harry Wait the convenient villain so the real issue stays buried: he requested ballots in the names of Robin Vos and Cory Mason to show Wisconsin’s voter registration system could be exploited. The jury convicted him on two misdemeanor election fraud charges and one felony identity theft charge, while acquitting him of a second identity theft count—a split result officials can use to look measured while keeping scrutiny off the system itself. The message is obvious: expose a vulnerability, and the institutions will make an example of you rather than answer for it.
